scope: Time-boxed search (about 20 minutes, 19:08-19:28 on 25 October) for established snowflake melting physics with Earth support and for observed Earth melting-layer depths, for the melting of lunar snowflakes below the freezing level (melting.py).
finding: Mitra and co-authors' (1990) single-flake melting model, which Frick, Seifert and Wernli (2013) give in full, supplies the melting rate, the melting flake's capacitance, density and fall speed; the onset of melting follows the ice-bulb criterion of Heymsfield and co-authors (2021); observed Earth melting depths and temperatures, and Matsuo and Sasyo's (1981) computed onset depths, serve as the Earth check.
external_bytes: No papers or datasets added to the repository. Retrieved PDFs are kept, with these hashes, in the agent's folder on the research drive (atmosphere-snow/claude-agent-3/literature).
model_changes: The vapour diffusivity is Massman's (1998) fit, which the rain solver (atmosphere/rain/drops.py) takes since 25 October in place of its Chapman-Enskog value, 17.6% lower.

sources.authors: Claudia Frick, Axel Seifert and Heini Wernli
sources.title: A bulk parametrization of melting snowflakes with explicit liquid water fraction for the COSMO model
sources.publication: Geoscientific Model Development 6, 1925-1939 (2013), doi:10.5194/gmd-6-1925-2013, CC BY 3.0
sources.obtained: Full PDF fetched 25 October 2026 and read through pdftotext.
sources.reading_extent: Abstract, introduction, section 2.1-2.2 (the single-flake model, eqs. 1-17 and Fig. 1), the melting-layer statistics of section 3.

quantities.melting_rate: dm_w/dt = (4 pi C F_v / L_F) [k (T - T0) + (L_v D_v / R_v)(e/T - e_sw(T0)/T0)] (eqs. 1, 7)
quantities.capacitance: C_m = alpha_cap(l) D_m/2 sqrt(1 - a^2) / arcsin sqrt(1 - a^2), alpha_cap = 0.8 + 0.2 l (eqs. 9, 13)
quantities.density_and_span: rho_m = rho_s + (rho_w - rho_s) l, rho_s capped at 500 kg/m3; D_m = (6 m / (pi a rho_m))^(1/3) (eqs. 10-12)
quantities.fall_speed: v_m = v_s + (v_r - v_s) Psi(l), Psi = 0.246 l + 0.754 l^7, fitted to Mitra's Fig. 2 (eqs. 14, 15)
quantities.ventilation: Hall and Pruppacher (1976), Reynolds number interpolated linearly in l between the dry flake and the drop, maximum dimension as length (eqs. 16, 17)
quantities.cosmo_case: Snow reaches up to 70 hPa below the top of the melting layer with the new scheme, against 30 hPa with the standard one (model result)

sources.use: The melting stage of melting.py, equation by equation.
sources.limit: A model paper: its single-flake parametrization rests on Mitra's laboratory flakes, which were centimetre-sized; the lunar flakes reach 10-20 cm and Reynolds numbers of several thousand.

sources.authors: S. K. Mitra, O. Vohl, M. Ahr and H. R. Pruppacher
sources.title: A wind tunnel and theoretical study of the melting behavior of atmospheric ice particles. IV: Experiment and theory for snow flakes
sources.obtained: Not obtained: the publisher's site refused automated access. Read through Frick and co-authors (2013), who give its model and its fall-speed data, through Heymsfield and co-authors (2021), and through its abstract (search result text).

quantities.experiment: Natural and laboratory aggregates melted in free fall in the Mainz vertical wind tunnel in air warmed at the rate a falling flake meets, at 90% relative humidity (Heymsfield and co-authors 2021); melting began when the flake's surface reached 0 C
quantities.theory: An oblate spheroid with the meltwater soaking into the flake; computed melting distances agreed with radar observations (abstract)

sources.use: The origin of the model melting.py follows.
sources.limit: Unread directly; its tables of melting distance are not checked here.

sources.authors: Andrew J. Heymsfield, Aaron Bansemer, Alexander Theis and Carl Schmitt
sources.title: Survival of snow in the melting layer: relative humidity influence
sources.publication: Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences 78, 1823-1845 (2021), doi:10.1175/JAS-D-20-0353.1
sources.obtained: Full PDF (the publisher's version deposited at OSTI) fetched 25 October 2026 and read through pdftotext.
sources.reading_extent: Abstract, introduction, section 3a (the ice-bulb criterion and the spiral descents), section 4 (discussion and the fitted relations).

quantities.onset: Melting begins where the ice-bulb temperature reaches 0 C; RH_IB(1000 hPa) = 100 - 12.67 T, RH_IB(500 hPa) = 100 - 9.3 T (eqs. 2a, 2b)
quantities.completion: Melting completes 1-2 C warmer than the onset, by particle type and largest size
quantities.kwajex_spirals: In moist spirals melting was first seen at +1 C and was complete by +3 C
quantities.willis_heymsfield_1989: Melting nearly complete by +3 C, some large aggregates reaching +5 C and warmer as ice (cited)
quantities.wolfensberger_2016: Median melting-layer depths from radar of 350, 300, 350 and 325 m at Davos, Payerne, Ardeche and Iowa (cited)
quantities.warmest_snow: Snow observed as warm as +7 C in dry air

sources.use: The onset criterion and the Earth check's observed targets.
sources.limit: Aircraft spirals and surface reports at Earth's pressures and lapse rates; Wolfensberger's and Willis and Heymsfield's values are taken as this paper cites them.

sources.title: Melting of snowflakes below freezing level in the atmosphere
sources.publication: Journal of the Meteorological Society of Japan 59, 10-25 (1981)
sources.obtained: Full PDF fetched 25 October 2026 and read through pdftotext.
sources.reading_extent: Abstract, the model's assumptions (section 3), the results on temperature, water content and fall speed by distance below the freezing level (section 4).

quantities.lapse: 6 K/km, relative humidity constant below the freezing level
quantities.saturated: Flakes of melted diameter 1-5 mm complete melting within several hundred metres; the melting layer deepens with flake size and density
quantities.fall_speed: Nearly constant before melting in subsaturated air, rising rapidly once melting proceeds

sources.use: Computed onset depths the Earth check compares with.
sources.limit: A model with an empirical melting-rate formula, not observations.

sources.authors: Jussi Leinonen and Annakaisa von Lerber
sources.title: Snowflake melting simulation using smoothed particle hydrodynamics
sources.publication: Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres 123, 1811-1825 (2018), doi:10.1002/2017JD027909
sources.obtained: Not obtained: the publisher's site refused automated access. Abstract as search results give it.

quantities.meltwater: Meltwater gathers first in the concave parts of the surface, the pools merge and form a shell round an ice core, and the flake becomes a drop; unrimed flakes show surface water early

sources.use: Supports splitting the melting flake's vapour exchange between exposed ice and water.

sources.title: A review of the molecular diffusivities of H2O, CO2, CH4, CO, O3, SO2, NH3, N2O, NO, and NO2 in air, O2 and N2 near STP
sources.obtained: The paper itself not retrieved. Its fit, 0.2178 cm2/s at 273.15 K and 1 atm with the temperature exponent constrained at 1.81 and an absolute uncertainty of 7%, confirmed on 25 October 2026 as quoted by a later review (Comparison of approaches for measuring the mass accommodation coefficient for the condensation of water, J. Phys. Chem. A, 2013; PMC3600786), search-result text.
sources.use: Vapour diffusivity in the rain solver, and through it in melting.py.
sources.limit: Secondary only; the 7% uncertainty is far smaller than the 17.6% by which the rain solver's kinetic theory falls below it.

quantities.data_range: 273.15-373.15 K, corrected to 1 atm by the inverse pressure law
quantities.uncertainty: 7%, the largest difference between the data and the fit
